title: Inheritance vs Composition (when to use what)

content.title: Inheritance vs Composition (when to use what)

blocks.content: Two ways to reuse code. One question: which one to pick? The answer depends on a single test and getting it wrong leads to brittle, unmaintainable code.
1. The Core Idea
One Question Decides Everything
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423484184-56561067.png
Inheritance ("IS-A" Relationship)
["Use when one class is a specialized version of another.","Example: Dog is an Animal → Dog inherits Animal's properties and behavior."]
items: Use when one class is a specialized version of another.
Example: Dog is an Animal → Dog inherits Animal's properties and behavior.

blocks.content: Composition ("HAS-A" Relationship)
["Use when one class contains or uses another class.","Example: Car has an Engine → Car uses Engine to perform engine-related work."]
items: Use when one class contains or uses another class.
Example: Car has an Engine → Car uses Engine to perform engine-related work.

blocks.content:
THE LISKOV TEST: USE THIS EVERY TIME

"Can I replace every use of the parent with the child and have everything still work correctly?"

If YES → inheritance is safe.
If NO → use composition.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423484568-26628815.png

["Inheritance (IS-A): Dog is an Animal, so Dog automatically gets Animal's properties and behaviors.
","Composition (HAS-A): Car has an Engine, so Car uses an Engine object to perform engine-related tasks.
"]
items: Inheritance (IS-A): Dog is an Animal, so Dog automatically gets Animal's properties and behaviors.
Composition (HAS-A): Car has an Engine, so Car uses an Engine object to perform engine-related tasks.

blocks.content: 2. When To Use Inheritance
Use Inheritance When ALL Three Are True
Think of these as three gates all must be open before you choose inheritance.

["Genuine IS-A Relationship: Use inheritance only when the child is truly a specialized form of the parent. Example: Dog is an Animal.
","Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): The child object should be usable anywhere the parent object is expected without causing incorrect behavior. Example: A Dog should work wherever an Animal is expected.
","Shared Implementation: Use inheritance when multiple child classes can reuse common code from the parent, instead of duplicating the same logic in each class. Example: All shapes share a commondescribe()implementation."]
items: Genuine IS-A Relationship: Use inheritance only when the child is truly a specialized form of the parent. Example: Dog is an Animal.

Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): The child object should be usable anywhere the parent object is expected without causing incorrect behavior. Example: A Dog should work wherever an Animal is expected.

Shared Implementation: Use inheritance when multiple child classes can reuse common code from the parent, instead of duplicating the same logic in each class. Example: All shapes share a commondescribe()implementation.

blocks.content: The Shape class is a parent (base) class that contains functionality common to all shapes. It stores the colour property and provides a describe() method that every shape can use.
Since every shape calculates its area differently, the area() method is declared as abstract, forcing each child class to provide its own implementation.
Circle and Rectangle inherit from Shape. A circle calculates its area using the circle formula, while a rectangle calculates its area using the rectangle formula.
Both classes automatically inherit the colour field and the describe() method, so they only need to implement the part that is unique to them: the area calculation.
This is a good example of inheritance because all three inheritance checks pass. First, a Circle and Rectangle genuinely are Shapes.

Second, a Circle can be used anywhere a Shape is expected, satisfying the Liskov Substitution Principle. Third, the child classes reuse the shared describe() implementation from the parent instead of duplicating the same code.
When we write Shape s = new Circle(5.0);, the variable type is Shape but the actual object is a Circle.
Calling s.describe() executes the shared describe() method from Shape, which internally calls area().
Due to polymorphism, the Circle version of area() is executed, producing the correct result for a circle. This demonstrates inheritance, code reuse, and runtime polymorphism working together.
ANALOGY: INHERITING A HOUSE

You inherit a house and get everything the furniture you love AND the leaky roof you don't. You didn't choose. Inheritance works the same: you get the full package useful methods, irrelevant fields, hidden dependencies. Only use it when you genuinely want the whole package.
3. When To Use Composition
- Use Composition in All Other Cases
If any of the three inheritance gates fails or if you need runtime flexibility, multiple behaviours, or easy testing composition is the answer.

["Case 1: Multiple behaviours needed
"]
Java has no multiple inheritance. A Duck that needs to fly AND swim can't extend two classes but it can hold both behaviours as fields.

["Case 2: Behaviour must change at runtime
"]
items: Case 2: Behaviour must change at runtime

blocks.content: Inheritance is fixed at compile time. Composition lets you swap the injected object at any point while the program runs.

["Case 3: No real \"is-a\" relationship
"]
"LoggingService is-a OrderService" makes no domain sense. A logger should wrap a service, not inherit from it.

["Case 4: Easy testability needed
"]
With composition, inject a fake object in tests. With inheritance, you're stuck testing the whole chain together.
composition is used instead of inheritance. A Duck does not inherit flying or swimming behavior. Instead, it has aFlyBehaviour object and a SwimBehaviour object.
Whenever the duck needs to fly or swim, it delegates that work to these behavior objects.
This design allows different ducks to have different behaviors without creating a large inheritance hierarchy.

For example, a MallardDuck can use FlapWings for flying, while a RubberDuck can use NoFly. Both are still ducks, but their behaviors are composed from separate objects rather than being hardcoded through inheritance.
A major advantage of composition is flexibility. The behavior can be changed at runtime.

In the example, the mallard duck initially flies using FlapWings, but after getting injured, its flying behavior is replaced with NoFly using setFly(). No new subclass is needed; only the behavior object is swapped.
This is a good use of composition because a duck is not a FlyBehaviour and not a SwimBehaviour.
Instead, a duck hasflying and swimming capabilities. Composition keeps behaviors independent, reusable, and easy to change, making the design more flexible than inheritance.
ANALOGY: BUILDING A PC

You assemble a PC by picking exactly the parts you want CPU, GPU, RAM. You can upgrade the GPU without touching the CPU. None of the parts inherit from each other. That's composition: independent, swappable pieces assembled into something capable.
4. The Classic Mistake
This is the most famous example of inheritance going wrong. Geometrically, a square is a rectangle. But in code, it breaks the contract.
1. Why Square extends Rectangle Fails
A Square changes the behavior of setWidth() and setHeight() because its width and height must always remain equal.

Code written for a Rectangle expects width and height to change independently. When a Square is used in place of a Rectangle, that expectation breaks, violating the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP).
2. Why the Interface Solution Works
Instead of inheritance, bothRectangleandSquareindependently implement the sameShapeinterface.
Each class calculates its area in its own way without pretending to be the other. This avoids broken behavior and keeps the design correct and flexible.
5. The Decision Table
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423484803-810035679.png
When in doubt use composition. It's always easier to add delegation than to untangle an inheritance hierarchy later. Inheritance is a permanent commitment; composition can be changed anytime.
6. The Three Rules

["Use inheritance only when: it's genuinely is-a, Liskov substitution holds, and subclasses share real implementation code.","Use composition when: you need multiple behaviours, runtime flexibility, adding features without changing existing classes, or when there's no true is-a.","The Liskov test is your single most reliable signal if substituting the child for the parent breaks anything, don't use inheritance."]
items: Use inheritance only when: it's genuinely is-a, Liskov substitution holds, and subclasses share real implementation code.
Use composition when: you need multiple behaviours, runtime flexibility, adding features without changing existing classes, or when there's no true is-a.
The Liskov test is your single most reliable signal if substituting the child for the parent breaks anything, don't use inheritance.
